To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ostensible benefits of Catholic education depend critically on the validity one instrument (having nearby access to a private school) and that this benefit is fragile.
the Catholic school advantage is fragile and that it is not a robust finding.

Catholic schools have a small, positive effect on student achievement; this effect is robust to the inclusion of student fixed effects; the effect is not robust to the inclusion and use of an instrument; the instrument is invalid, but the degree to which the instrument is invalid is not known.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what constitutes evidence in observational studies.
the design of observational studies of the effectiveness of Catholic schools.
the design of observational studies, with particular attention to the use of multiple instruments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results from this analysis are consistent with Catholic education providing no benefit to students, and that the results are also consistent with Catholic schools providing a substantial benefit to students, with the latter conclusion depending upon the validity of one particular instrument.
the evidence is not strong enough to rule out a large positive effect of Catholic education, or a large negative effect.
the Catholic schools do no more than the public schools, and may do less, to improve students’ test scores.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that the evidence factors approach is a useful and powerful way to strengthen causal conclusions in non-experimental studies.
we show how to use multiple instruments to strengthen evidence factors and to construct multiple evidence factors from multiple instruments.
the evidence factors approach can be useful, but the usefulness is limited by the quality of the instruments.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the methods we propose are not a panacea for the problems that plague observational studies, but they do provide a useful tool for assessing the sensitivity of a study to various assumptions and for assessing the degree of concordance across different assumptions.

multiple instruments plus control groups can be used as evidence factors in a design sensitivity analysis, and that the sensitivity of the evidence factors can be studied by simulations that examine the sensitivity of each factor to the assumptions underlying it.
the use of multiple instruments plus control groups is a promising way to strengthen causal conclusions, but that it is not a panacea.
